en: The Vyāliśikṣā, Chapter One: The Commencement of the Vyāliśikṣā.
Permitted by Brahmā in ancient times, I shall proclaim the Vyāliśikṣā.
I shall describe that which is endowed with a thousand faces and the Sūtra;
therein, first, the measurement and characteristics of the solid (ghana), as well as the method for the solid and likewise the joints of the solid.
All such matters as these, I shall now declare in their entirety:
in the *ghana* [meter], there should be twelve *sandhis* and one should state thirteen *padas*;
in the *trikrama*, the *sandhi* is likewise prescribed as being seventeenfold.
One should recite that [text] consisting of eighteen sections, and therein it is prescribed:
whoever should chant it with its proper accents, according to the rule, as it truly is, and with its defining characteristics—even he shall attain that state of Brahman. 4–5.
First, the two-word phrase is repeated six times joined like matted hair;
thereafter, the single word is repeated twice again.
In the reverse order, however, the middle word is recited only once.
Having first explained those two types in direct order according to their sequence,
one should then immediately begin with the middle term;
as before, one should perform the conjunction, and thus the "solid" (ghana) is prescribed.

Thus ends the Vyāliśikṣā. Having placed the illustrious feet of Śrī Nṛhari in his heart, [the author] composed this commentary on the eight *vibhaktis* of the Ṛgveda, which is worthy of being recited as Vedic verse.
With the approval of the teacher Vyāḍi, the mendicant named Madhusūdana, born from the body of the venerable preceptor Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
proclaims this great work of mine, which is naturally pure, captivating, dispelling ignorance like nectar, and removing the doubts of those who serve it.
May she, who steals away the speech of rival scholars and sports daily in the minds of those learned in the Vedas, become [the ornament] of the knowers of Vedic wisdom—
she whose dense locks are like the matted hair, garlands, staff-lines, chariot-banners, and crests of the gods.
The eight well-known modifications (vikāras) are produced by relying on the sequence [of syllables].

First, there are five sequences beginning with "two-footed" (dvipadā), which proceed from direct order (krama) and then from reverse order (vyutkrama); these, when uttered again in direct order, are brought to the state of "braided hair" (jaṭā) by the wise.
Succession (anukrama), emergence (utkrama), transgression (vyutkrama), advancement (abhikrama),
and transition (saṃkrama)— these five sequences are taught regarding the *jaṭā*;
in the sequences of the three-footed [meter] beginning with the syllable 'ā', the syllable 'ā' is as before.
The pair of words is not a tautology, nor is there a confusion of two words within the three-word sequence,
because it proceeds as a single causal unit; thus, it does not deserve to be called "entangled" (*jaṭā*),
just as in the case of the three-word sequence beginning with *sānusvārākāra*.
To eliminate the misconception that there are two sequences, there is the encircling of the middle word.

In the *jaṭā* arrangement, the two sequences are subject to the characteristics defined by the *Prātiśākhya*; however, when they are reversed, that [Prātiśākhya rule] is not considered applicable, and in that case, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is held to be the authority.

Having abandoned the changes of *ṣ* to *s*, *ṇ* to *n*, *d* to *t*, and *g* to *t*, as well as the qualities of shortness and length according to the rules of *saṃhitā*, one should recite [the mantra] word by word, even when they appear out of their regular order.
The vowel *o* occurring in *saṃhitā* should become the word-form *au*.

In some cases, when there is a transposition (*vyutkrama*), it should be expressed as such; however, in the case of *jaṭā*, it occurs only through the process of *auttva*. Since the final element is the end in the regular order (*krama*) and the first element is the end in the transposed order (*vyutkrama*), their repetition is appropriate; it is not so in the middle, nor in the case of triplets (*trikrama*) and the like.

In the inversion of sequences such as the *trikrama* and others, one attains the middle word—the unrevolved dharma—by excluding the middle word and uniting the preceding and following words. 12. [This occurs] by setting aside the middle word and through the oneness of the prior and subsequent words.

That single step which has been prescribed for the procedure of *viloma-jaṭā* (the inverted matted-hair arrangement), one should utter after first discarding that which arose before the initiated step and was excluded from it;
then, one should utter the word "Śunaḥśepa" joined with the state of oneness. 13–14.
For indeclinables ending in *o*, there is *pragṛhya* status when they are reversed; for vocatives ending in *o*, there is no *pragṛhya* status when they are not in their regular order.
Feminine stems ending in *ī* that consist of three syllables, as well as those ending in *ā*, are never *pragṛhya*.

Words ending in *ī*, *ū*, *e*, or *o*—even those consisting of three syllables—are likewise *pragṛhya* when they do not undergo euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in *saṃhitā*. However, dual endings (*dvivacana*) ending in *ī*, *ū*, *e*, or *o* are not so [treated]. 16–17.
This [particle] *uḥ* attains the status of a *pragṛhya* when followed by a vowel, just as *madanādi* does;
the *ukāra* preceded by *na* becomes one with the preceding *ukāra*, and even in the reversed form *nu u*, it correctly undergoes the substitution of *vā*. 18–19.
The *u*-vowel (*ukāra*), the *o*-vowel (*okāra*), and likewise the *au*-vowel (*aukāra*) are elided when followed by another vowel;
the *v*-vowel (*vakāra*) is elided before another [consonant], but it is not elided when followed by a vowel.
(20) The same applies to the *u*-vowels of *pragṛhya* words ending in three syllables and of vocatives (*āmantrita*).

However, it is stated that "in the case of a reversed word-sandhi (*viloma-padasandhi*), the status of being *pragṛhya* does not exist"; thus, even though the vowel *u* has become *o*, it would still be *pragṛhya*. That [vowel], which is seen as *avagraha* when there is no reversal, becomes [the subject] in the case of reversal.
Having attained oneness with the letter *i*, it possesses the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) form right there.
The first two words are pure, while the subsequent three words are either additional or all [of them] together are called the second half-verse (*ardharca*). 22–23.
There, having formed a *jaṭā* (conjunction) from the first pair of words and joined them together,
one should then utter the second [word] and the first of the *samaya* [words], followed by the *jaṭā*; then, throughout the entire latter half-verse, one should recite the *saṃhitā*.

If one should utter a pure word, having taken the *saṃhitā* as the limit at the beginning of the three words or at the first two words of the *samaya*, then, having stated that single pure word which serves as the limit for the purity, one should thereafter state the *saṃhitā*. 25–26.
Having joined the final and penultimate pure [syllables] with the last word of the *samaya*, and having uttered the *jaṭā*, one should encircle the pure word.
Wherever these two—the first and the last—are purified, in that very place [these syllables are applied]. 27.

One should explain the *jaṭā* by joining it with the first and last [syllables] of the *samaya*. However, wherever there are two pure *pada*s at the beginning and middle, the rule for the *jaṭā* consists of the first [syllable] joined with the first syllable of the *samaya* that is fixed upon it.
When the first part of the subsequent *samaya* is joined with the middle, that is the procedure for the *jaṭā*.
Where there is the preceding *samaya*, one should perform the *jaṭā* of the two pure parts while reciting the *saṃhitā* up to the limit of the second [part] of the pure portions. 29–30.

Where the first part (the *ādyāṃśa*) is pure and the subsequent part (*uttarāṃśaka*) is the *samaya*, one who is skilled in the transformation of *jaṭā* should subsequently join it with the final portion of the previous part and the first foot of the *samaya*; therein lies the *jaṭā*. 31.
The *pluti* is heard even in cases of transposition; in *saṃhitā*, *pada*, *krama*, and *jaṭā*, seven types of *svarita* occur, as well as in reverse order (*vilomaka*).
Furthermore, there are *tirovirāma*, *tairovyañjana*, and *pādavṛttaka*.
*Jātya*, *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, and *praśliṣṭa*—these are remembered [as the types of *sandhi*].
That which has a pause (*virāma*) concealed (*tiras*), begins with a high pitch (*uccais*), and starts with the emission (*sarga*) of a single syllable, is considered *prastuta*;
as in "pra" and "ca" at the beginning of a phrase, it is a pause preceded by concealment (*tiraḥpūrva*). 33–34.

That which follows an acute accent (*udātta*) other than a prefix (*upasarga*) is traditionally known as *taitro-vyajjana*; it is said to occur in cases of transposition, as in "hīle purohitam" [where the order is reversed]. 35.
A circumflex (*svarita*) produced by a hiatus (*vivṛtti*) is designated by the name *pādavṛtta*. 36.
That which is born of its own nature (jātyaḥ), self-sounding (svāraḥ), or unprecedented (apūrvaḥ), or preceded by a low note (nīcapūrvakaḥ);
or that which ends in 'va', 'anta', or 'yakāra'—where is the example of such a group? Those that are unprecedented or preceded by a low note have within them the form of another low note.

The *edotau* (e, o, ai, au) are *abhinihita*; this is the illustration thereof. Alternatively, the vowel *u*, or the vowel *i* preceded by a low-pitched (*nīca*) vowel, when combined with a high-pitched (*udātta*) vowel—whether long or short—[becomes an *abhinihita*]. 38.
When there is a conjunction (*yoga*), the two [vowels] that follow it are *kṣaipra*; examples are *nyūṣu* and *nvasya*.
(39) A short vowel preceded by a non-low (*apūrva*) or low (*nīca*) vowel, when followed by a shorter vowel, becomes *abhinihita*; examples are *ināyuk*, *praśliṣṭa*, *tāmābhi*, and *idamvīdam*. (40)

Among the four types of tremors, whichever tremor or its absence may occur during the transition [of breath], it is equal when two and a half *mātrās* have elapsed; these are the *jāti*, *akṣepa*, and *dīrghaka*. 41.

In the first part there should be two morae (mātrās), and in the latter part half a mora. The *kṣaipra*, *jātya*, *praśliṣṭa*, and *abhinihita* [svaritas] likewise possess a duration of four morae; they are characterized by the low (*anudātta*), high (*udātta*), and depressed (*nīca*) accents. 42–43.
The first portion, lasting for one and a half mātrās, is unaccented (anudātta).
The middle portion, lasting for one mātrā, is high-pitched (udātta), and the final portion, lasting for one and a half mātrās, is low-pitched (anudātta).
There is a modulation (kampana) of the *jātya* and other accents when an udātta or svarita follows.

Since a word is observed to be accented (*udātta*) immediately after a preceding *abhinihita* [sandhi], a tremor (*kampa*) characterized by low, high, and low pitches should be performed there, but not in every respect. Furthermore, the four types of *svarita* accents undergo tremor due to specific causes.

When these [elements] have become the objects of expression within a *jaṭā* consisting of sequential order and so forth, one should state the half-verse by reversing the order from beginning to end; thus, one should lead the end to the beginning, and this is celebrated as the *kramamālā*. 46–47.
The noble ones declare that the matted locks (*jaṭā*) are indeed the crest (*śikhā*) following the *pada* [mantra].
One should recite the sequence of two, three, four, and five *padas* in order; having reversed each one individually, they call it again the line (*rekhā*) in due order. 48–49.
One should correctly state the sequence from the beginning and conclude at the end; that which is recited within a *varga* or a *ṛc* is known as a *dhvaja*.
Having stated the sequence and then reversing it, one should again state the subsequent sequence.

The *kramadaṇḍa* is defined as follows: having recited [the verse] by quarters (*pādaśas*) or by half-verses (*ardharcaśas*), the chariot proceeds like a staff (*daṇḍavat*) through their simultaneous utterance. Having recited the crest-verse (*śikhā*) and then reversing it, one should again recite three words.
The mass of matted hair is declared to be Śikha; thus one should recite these eight transformations (vikṛtis). 53.
By this description of the nature of the eight transformations composed by me, may the victorious Viṣṇu, O Goddess Bhavānī, be pleased. 54.
Thus ends the commentary on the Eight Transformations composed by the venerable Madhusūdana.
